title: Male and female, concordance of the adjective

blocks.text: Each Arabic name is masculine or feminine, and the adjective follows: ⁧مَدِينَةٌ كَبِيرَةٌ⁩ A big city. ⁧بَيْتٌ كَبِيرٌ⁩ It's a big house. This unity teaches you to recognize gender, to form feminine and to describe people, places and objects. It lasts two weeks: the first for the rules, the second to enlarge the descriptive vocabulary and write the first descriptions.

rows: 12–14 hours · two weeks (weeks 15–16 of the calendar)

blocks.text: Materials This unit, Anki deck A1 (tag A1-03), voice synthesis script, tutor session in the second week
Targets. At the end of the lesson you know:
1. recognize the kind of a name by form and know the female without ⁧ة⁩ more frequent;
2. to form the female adjectives and professional names;
3. put the adjective after the name and accord it in the genre, even with two adjectives;
4. Use the adjective as a predicate ( ⁧هِيَ طَوِيلَةٌ⁩ ) and strengthen it with ⁧جِدًّا⁩ ;
5. describe two people and one city in 40 words;
6. recognize when listening if you talk about a man or a woman.
Two-week plan.

What to notice. ⁧مَنْ⁩ You'll study it in A1-06: here is a fixed block. ⁧صَغِيرٌ⁩ the name of the brother means "young" or "little girl." ⁧أُمِّي⁩ , ⁧أَخِي⁩ , ⁧بِنْتِي⁩ have the suffix -ī Mine/my. Luca uses ⁧مَا شَاءَ اللهُ⁩ ( A1-01) to compliment the child: it is the usual way of praising a child without attracting the evil eye, an attention widespread in many Arab families.
In Arabic there is no neutral: every name is male ( ⁧مُذَكَّر⁩ muḏakkar ) or female ( ⁧مُؤَنَّث⁩ muʾannaṯ ). Male does not have a particular sign; women, in the vast majority of cases, end up ⁧ة⁩ .

They are a few words, but very frequent. Learn them by their kind.

Because you need it. In reading their own names, in A2, you'll see ⁧حَمْزَة⁩ and ⁧أُسَامَة⁩ are common male names: do not attribute them to a woman for ⁧ة⁩ Final.
For adjectives and person names you add ⁧ة⁩ to the male. In front of the ⁧ة⁩ the last consonant takes the fatḥa.
Attention to the words in -iyy and the šadda. In ⁧مُهِمّ⁩ and ⁧شُرْطِيّ⁩ the šadda remains and the fatḥa go over the double letter:

Exception to recognize. The adjectives of color and physical defect have a different feminine: ⁧أَحْمَر⁩ aḥmar Red-red → ⁧حَمْرَاء⁩ ḥamrāʾ . You will study them in A2; For now know that they exist. The ⁧ة⁩ paused and connected. In pause we read -a ( ⁧كَبِيرَة⁩ kabīra ); Inside the sentence one reads -at more desinence ( ⁧كَبِيرَةٌ جِدًّا⁩ kabīratun ǧiddan ).
Attributional adjective. It follows the name, always, and takes its kind (and desinence, which here is -a):
⁧حَرْبٌ طَوِيلَةٌ⁩ ḥarbun ṭawīla a long war ( ⁧حَرْب⁩ is female)
Predicted adjective. After a pronoun or proper name, the adjective itself forms the nominal phrase (A1-02):

Because the adjective goes later. In Arabic the name comes first and what qualifies it follows: it is a fixed order, not stylistic. Beautiful city with the adjective in front ( ⁧جَمِيلَةٌ مَدِينَةٌ⁩ ) is not an Arabic phrase.

More adjectives are put one after the other, all agreed: ⁧مَدِينَةٌ قَدِيمَةٌ جَمِيلَةٌ⁩ It is an ancient and beautiful city. As preached they bind with ⁧وَ⁩ : ⁧القَاهِرَةُ كَبِيرَةٌ وَقَدِيمَةٌ⁩ . ⁧جِدًّا⁩ ǧiddan "Much" goes after the adjective: ⁧كَبِيرٌ جِدًّا⁩ Very big. It doesn't change for the genre. ⁧لٰكِنْ⁩ lākin "but" combines two sentences: . ⁧البَيْتُ صَغِيرٌ، لٰكِنْ هُوَ جَمِيلٌ⁩ In front of the article he took the support: ⁧لٰكِنِ الجَوُّ بَارِدٌ⁩ lākini l-ǧawwu bārid It's cold, though.
